items.title: Switches and markets
items.prose: A strategy has 4 filters, each switched on or off, and runs in one of 5 markets.
items.question: How many different set-ups are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each filter is a stage with 2 choices, and the market is one more stage.

byKey.one-switch: You treated the 4 filters as one on or off switch. Each filter is its own stage.
byKey.times-four: You multiplied 4 filters by 2 states. Each filter doubles the count, so it is $2^4$, not $4 \times 2$.
byKey.added: You added the choices. The filters and the market are stages, so multiply.
byKey.no-switch: You counted the markets only. Each filter doubles the count.

explain.text: Each filter doubles the count: $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16$. The market multiplies by 5. So there are $16 \times 5 = 80$ set-ups.

items.title: A PIN that cannot start with 0
items.prose: A bank's PIN has 4 digits, no digit repeated, and the first digit may not be 0.
items.question: How many PINs are allowed?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill the first digit first, with its own rule, then the rest.

byKey.ignored: That counts PINs that start with 0 too. The first digit has only 9 choices.
byKey.no-zero-anywhere: You removed 0 from every place. Only the first digit may not be 0.
byKey.lost-zero: You gave the second digit 8 choices. After the first digit, 0 becomes available, so 9 digits are left.

explain.text: The first digit has 9 choices, 1 to 9. The second may be 0 but not the first digit: 9 choices. Then 8 and 7, so $9 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 4536$.

items.title: Strong weeks
items.prose: A stock is up or down on each of the 5 trading days of a week. Call a week strong if it has at least 4 up days.
items.question: How many up-down patterns give a strong week?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At least 4 means exactly 4 or exactly 5.

byKey.only-four: You counted exactly 4 up days. A week with all 5 up is strong too.
byKey.only-five: You counted only the all-up week. Exactly 4 up days also counts.
byKey.wrong-r: You worked out $\binom{5}{2}$ or $\binom{5}{3}$. Strong weeks have 4 or 5 up days.

explain.text: Exactly 4 up days: $\binom{5}{4} = 5$, one for each choice of down day. Exactly 5: $\binom{5}{5} = 1$. These cases cannot overlap, so they add to 6.

items.title: Pairs in a correlation matrix
items.prose: A correlation matrix for $n$ stocks needs one number for each pair of different stocks. The pair (A, B) is the same as (B, A).
items.question: Write the number of pairs in terms of $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count ordered pairs, then divide by the 2 orders of each pair.

byKey.ordered: You counted ordered pairs. (A, B) and (B, A) are one pair, so halve it.
byKey.square: You halved $n^2$, which includes each stock paired with itself.

explain.text: Ordered pairs of different stocks: $n(n-1)$. Each pair appears twice, so there are $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$. For 100 stocks that is 4950 correlations to estimate.

items.title: The symmetry, from the formula
items.prose: We want to show $\binom{n}{n-r} = \binom{n}{r}$ from the formula $\binom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$.
items.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: Simplify the last bracket, since $n - (n - r) = r$.
The two factors below can be multiplied in either order, so this is $\dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!} = \binom{n}{r}$.

feedback.correct: Substitute, simplify, then reorder the product.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by putting $n - r$ into the formula.

byKey.swap: Reordering the factors is the last step. First you need both factors in view.
byKey.simp: You can only simplify the bracket once it has appeared. Substitute first.

explain.text: Substituting $n - r$ for $r$ gives $(n-r)!$ and $r!$ below the line. Swapping their order gives the formula for $\binom{n}{r}$. The counting reason is the same: choosing who is in fixes who is out.

items.title: A committee with a chair
items.prose: A risk committee has 4 members chosen from 10 traders. One of the 4 is then named chair.
items.question: How many ways are there to form the committee and name its chair?

options.why: You chose the committee but did not name a chair. Each committee has 4 choices of chair.
You ranked all four members. Only the chair is special; the other three are equal.
You picked the chair from all 10. The chair must be one of the 4 members.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the 4 members, then choose the chair from among them.

explain.text: Choose the committee, $\binom{10}{4} = 210$, then its chair, 4 ways: 840. Or choose the chair first, 10 ways, then 3 more members, $\binom{9}{3} = 84$: also 840. Two routes agreeing is a good check.

items.title: Three hedges in a row
items.prose: Seven orders are sent one at a time. Three of them are hedges and must be sent consecutively, in any order among themselves.
items.question: How many sending orders are allowed?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tape the three hedges into one block, then count both levels.

byKey.block-fixed: You lined up the 5 units but kept the hedges in one order. The block's insides can be arranged in $3! = 6$ ways.
byKey.ignored: That is every sending order, including those that split the hedges.
byKey.two-way: You let the block flip only two ways. Three hedges have $3! = 6$ orders inside the block.

explain.text: The hedge block and the 4 other orders make 5 units: $5! = 120$. Inside the block the hedges go in $3! = 6$ orders. So there are $120 \times 6 = 720$ allowed sending orders.

items.title: Weighted and unweighted portfolios
items.prompt:
A fund picks 4 stocks from a shortlist of 12.

(a) The portfolio is equal-weighted. How many portfolios are possible?

(b) Instead, the 4 stocks get weights of 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%, one weight each. How many portfolios are possible now?

(c) Explain, without dividing your answers, why (b) is exactly 24 times (a).

(d) The fund must hold its flagship stock, which is on the shortlist. How many equal-weighted portfolios include it?
items.model:
**(a)** Order does not matter, because every stock gets the same weight. Ordered picks of 4 from 12 number $P(12, 4) = 12 \times 11 \times 10 \times 9 = 11\,880$. Each set of 4 stocks appears $4! = 24$ times among them. So there are $\binom{12}{4} = \dfrac{11\,880}{24} = 495$ portfolios.

**(b)** Now the weights are different, so order matters. Give the 40% weight first: 12 choices. Then 30%: 11 choices, 20%: 10, and 10%: 9. By the product rule there are $12 \times 11 \times 10 \times 9 = 11\,880$ portfolios, which is $P(12, 4) = \dfrac{12!}{8!}$.

**(c)** A weighted portfolio is made in two stages. First choose which 4 stocks to hold: 495 ways. Then hand the 4 different weights to those 4 stocks: $4! = 24$ ways, since the 40% weight has 4 choices, the 30% weight 3, and so on. The product rule gives $495 \times 24$, so (b) is exactly $4! = 24$ times (a).

**(d)** The flagship is fixed, so only 3 more stocks are chosen, from the other 11. That gives $\binom{11}{3} = \dfrac{11 \times 10 \times 9}{3!} = 165$ portfolios.

rubric.text: States that order does not matter in (a) because the weights are equal.
Finds $\binom{12}{4} = 495$, by dividing $P(12, 4)$ by $4!$ or by the formula.
States that order matters in (b) because the weights differ.
Finds $P(12, 4) = 11\,880$ by filling the weights in turn.
Explains (c) as two stages, choosing the stocks then assigning the weights in $4!$ ways, joined by the product rule.
Fixes the flagship in (d) and finds $\binom{11}{3} = 165$.
